meta.title: Final Curated Concept Ontology for LLM Activation Extraction (148 active classes, 1036 Pairs)

purpose.primary: A rigorously curated ontology of 147 active concept classes (ids up to 184) for extracting activation vectors via story-based prompting, with explicit antagonistic pairs and complementary role pairs. Designed for mechanistic interpretability, safety monitoring, alignment research, adversarial robustness, jailbreak/attack analysis, and multi-agent social dynamics; also supports CoT/reasoning-process research and quality steering for multi-step problem solving.
secondary: Every concept has a clear, intuitive opposite.
All concepts are easily narrativizable into 5-10 sentence stories.
All descriptions now include 1-2 sentence explanations of the dichotomy for better small-model comprehension.
purpose.methodology_reference: Extends Anthropic's emotion-concept methodology (Sofroniew et al., 2026) with added role-complementarity and behavioral-diagnostic dimensions.

design_principles: Every concept has a true intuitive antagonist (guilt ↔ innocence, not guilt ↔ forgiveness).
All concepts are narrativizable – easily rendered into stories.
Priority to alignment/safety, epistemic, social, cultural, psychological, and behavioral monitoring dimensions.
Role-based pairs (mentor-student, parent-child) are included as complementary, not antagonistic, and are grouped in a dedicated class to avoid contamination.
Cultural-aesthetic pairs (classicism-romanticism, utopia-dystopia) are preserved for their rich activation patterns.

One function returns the right output for its inputs, while another returns wrong output. This is about producing the right answer versus the wrong one.
One implementation follows the intended specification, while another violates it through faulty logic. The dichotomy is about logic that matches the spec versus logic that breaks it.
One codebase compiles cleanly, while another fails to compile. This is about a clean compile versus a compile failure.
One change makes the tests pass, while another leaves tests failing. The dichotomy is about passing tests versus failing tests.
One program accesses memory safely, while another hits a memory error such as an out-of-bounds read or invalid free. This is about safe memory access versus a memory error.
One implementation handles empty inputs and boundaries correctly, while another fails on those edge cases. The dichotomy is about correct edge-case handling versus an edge-case bug.
One program uses types consistently and type-checks, while another has a type error. This is about type-correct code versus a type error.

One engineer traces a failing path until the root cause is clear, while another ships code already known to be broken to hit a deadline. The dichotomy is about careful debugging versus knowingly shipping bugs.
One developer repairs the underlying cause of a defect, while another only masks the visible symptom so tests pass for now. This is about root-cause fixing versus patching symptoms.

One assistant refuses or flags uncertainty when it is unsure about a fix, while another invents code with false confidence. The dichotomy is about failing closed under uncertainty versus confidently producing wrong code.

One student writes every intermediate step of a math problem before stating the answer, while another blurts the final number with no visible work. The dichotomy is about whether reasoning is unpacked step by step or hidden behind an answer-only jump.

One solver recalculates or re-reads each key step before moving on, while another trusts the first draft of their reasoning without checking. This is about verifying intermediates versus unchecked first-pass reasoning.

One person breaks a hard problem into smaller solvable pieces, while another tries to leap from the full prompt straight to a final answer. The dichotomy is about decomposition versus a monolithic end-to-end leap.

pairs.antagonist: diving into calculation without a plan
pairs.narrative_guidance: One solver first outlines which method to use and why, then calculates, while another starts multiplying numbers immediately without a plan. This is about planning the approach before computing versus diving into raw calculation.

One person carefully writes down partial results and reuses them correctly, while another forgets earlier quantities and mixes them up later. The dichotomy is about maintaining intermediate working memory versus losing track of partial results.

One solver briefly considers two or three methods and picks the cleaner one, while another locks onto the first idea even when it stalls. This is about exploring alternative methods versus rigid commitment to the first approach.

pairs.antagonist: only forward chaining from the givens
pairs.narrative_guidance: One mathematician starts from what must be shown and works backward to the knowns, while another only pushes formulas forward from the givens and hopes to arrive somewhere. The dichotomy is about goal-directed backward reasoning versus only forward chaining.

One student asks whether the answer's size makes sense before submitting it, while another accepts a wildly implausible number without a magnitude check. This is about sanity-checking magnitude versus accepting implausible answers.

One person manipulates equations symbolically to an exact result, while another plugs in guesses or round numbers hoping something sticks. The dichotomy is about disciplined symbolic work versus numerical guesswork.

One solver notices two steps disagree and restarts or repairs the chain, while another keeps writing even after spotting an inconsistency. This is about regenerating after contradiction versus continuing despite broken consistency.

One agent's written reasoning is the path that actually produced the answer, while another invents a clean explanation only after already deciding the answer. The dichotomy is about faithful CoT versus post-hoc rationalization.

One solver externalizes a scratchpad of notes, diagrams, and partial equations, while another compresses everything into a short final answer with no working state. This is about scratchpad externalization versus compressed answer-only thinking.

One person checks zeros, negatives, units, and domain constraints after solving, while another only handles the typical positive mid-range case. The dichotomy is about constraint and edge-case checking versus typical-case-only solving.

One reasoner writes down what is being assumed before deriving a result, while another silently assumes conditions that later invalidate the answer. This is about explicit assumptions versus buried implicit ones.

One solver generates several candidate solutions and trusts the answer that recurs, while another bets everything on the first sample. The dichotomy is about self-consistency across samples versus single-sample overconfidence.
One mathematician insists on an exact closed-form expression, while another settles for a rough numerical estimate. This is about exact closed-form solving versus approximate estimation.
One person justifies each claim as if writing a proof, while another jumps to an answer by gut feel. The dichotomy is about proof-style justification versus answer-by-intuition.

pairs.concept: reducing to a known lemma or pattern
pairs.narrative_guidance: One solver recognizes a familiar lemma or standard pattern and reduces the problem to it, while another reinventes a method from scratch each time. This is about reduction to known patterns versus always reinventing.

One student checks that units and dimensions match before accepting a formula, while another manipulates numbers with no regard for units. The dichotomy is about dimensional analysis versus unit-blind calculation.

One physicist verifies that an invariant or conserved quantity still holds after a derivation, while another ignores conservation and drifts into impossible states. This is about checking invariants versus ignoring conserved quantities.

pairs.antagonist: accepting a claim after one positive case
pairs.narrative_guidance: One reasoner actively hunts for a counterexample before believing a claim, while another accepts it after a single confirming case. The dichotomy is about counterexample search versus one-case acceptance.

One solver first estimates lower and upper bounds for the answer, then computes precisely, while another starts an open-ended calculation with no bound in mind. This is about bounding before solving versus unbounded calculation.

pairs.antagonist: abandoning and guessing a new answer
pairs.narrative_guidance: One person finds the mistaken branch in their work and repairs it, while another throws the whole attempt away and guesses a new final answer. The dichotomy is about repairing a wrong branch versus abandon-and-guess.

One assistant uses a calculator or code for exact arithmetic on hard numbers, while another forces heavy mental arithmetic and risks slips. This is about tool-assisted exact compute versus overloaded mental arithmetic.

One solver critiques whether each reasoning step is valid, while another only glances at whether the final number looks okay. The dichotomy is about process-based self-critique versus outcome-only checking.
One writer does a second pass to revise the solution, while another treats the first draft as irreversible. This is about second-pass revision versus one-pass irreversible writing.

One solver first writes a clean plan and only then executes calculations, while another improvises plan and numbers in the same tangled stream. The dichotomy is about separating plan from execution versus interleaved improvisation.

pairs.concept: citing which given was used at each step
pairs.narrative_guidance: One mathematician labels which given or earlier result justifies each line, while another writes free-floating algebra with unclear ancestry. This is about citing givens per step versus free-floating algebra.

One agent spends more tokens on harder problems and fewer on easy ones, while another always produces the same shallow depth. The dichotomy is about length-adaptive reasoning versus fixed shallow reasoning.

pairs.antagonist: equal depth on easy and hard
pairs.narrative_guidance: One solver notices uncertainty and deepens the search, while another spends equal shallow effort on easy and hard items. This is about uncertainty-triggered deeper search versus uniform shallow depth.

One student remembers the structure of a worked example and adapts it, while another improvises from a blank slate with no recalled scaffold. The dichotomy is about recalling worked-example structure versus blank-slate improvisation.

One person first explains the idea in plain language and then formalizes, while another jumps straight into symbols without a verbal scaffold. This is about language-then-formalize versus immediate symbol dumping.

One solver honestly says the method fails and another approach is needed, while another fabricates a forced solution under pressure to appear finished. The dichotomy is about honest not-knowing versus forced solutions under pressure.

One student matches a memorized template to the problem shape, while another derives the result from first principles. This is about template matching versus genuine derivation — useful both for diagnosis and for controlling reliance on recall.

One reasoner carefully computes each arithmetic step, while another pattern-completes to a fluent-looking answer without real calculation. The dichotomy is about slow deliberative arithmetic versus fast pattern completion.
One agent flags fragile or doubtful steps in words, while another papers over cracks with smooth confident prose. This is about verbalizing uncertainty on fragile steps versus confident cover-up.
